stem: Suppose that the lower half of the concave mirror's reflecting surface in Fig. 9.6 is covered with an opaque (non-reflective) material. What effect will this have on the image of an object placed in front of the mirror?
solution: You may think that the image will now show only half of the object, but taking the laws of reflection to be true for all points of the remaining part of the mirror, the image will be that of the whole object. However, as the area of the reflecting surface has been reduced, the intensity of the image will be low (in this case, half).

stem: A mobile phone lies along the principal axis of a concave mirror, as shown in Fig. 9.7. Show by suitable diagram, the formation of its image. Explain why the magnification is not uniform. Will the distortion of image depend on the location of the phone with respect to the mirror?
solution: The ray diagram for the formation of the image of the phone is shown in Fig. 9.7. The image of the part which is on the plane perpendicular to principal axis will be on the same plane. It will be of the same size, i.e., \(\text{B}'\text{C} = \text{BC}\). You can yourself realise why the image is distorted.

stem: An object is placed at (i) \(10\,\text{cm}\), (ii) \(5\,\text{cm}\) in front of a concave mirror of radius of curvature \(15\,\text{cm}\). Find the position, nature, and magnification of the image in each case.
solution:
The focal length \(f = -15/2\,\text{cm} = -7.5\,\text{cm}\)

(i) The object distance \(u = -10\,\text{cm}\). Then Eq. (9.7) gives
\(\dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{1}{-10} = \dfrac{1}{-7.5}\)

or \(v = \dfrac{10 \times 7.5}{-2.5} = -30\,\text{cm}\)

The image is \(30\,\text{cm}\) from the mirror on the same side as the object.

Also, magnification \(m = -\dfrac{v}{u} = -\dfrac{(-30)}{(-10)} = -3\)

The image is magnified, real and inverted.

(ii) The object distance \(u = -5\,\text{cm}\). Then from Eq. (9.7),
\(\dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{1}{-5} = \dfrac{1}{-7.5}\)

or \(v = \dfrac{5 \times 7.5}{(7.5 - 5)} = 15\,\text{cm}\)

This image is formed at \(15\,\text{cm}\) behind the mirror. It is a virtual image.

Magnification \(m = -\dfrac{v}{u} = -\dfrac{15}{(-5)} = 3\)

The image is magnified, virtual and erect.

stem: Suppose while sitting in a parked car, you notice a jogger approaching towards you in the side view mirror of \(R = 2\,\text{m}\). If the jogger is running at a speed of \(5\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), how fast the image of the jogger appear to move when the jogger is (a) \(39\,\text{m}\), (b) \(29\,\text{m}\), (c) \(19\,\text{m}\), and (d) \(9\,\text{m}\) away.
solution:
From the mirror equation, Eq. (9.7), we get
\(v = \dfrac{fu}{u - f}\)

For convex mirror, since \(R = 2\,\text{m}\), \(f = 1\,\text{m}\). Then

for \(u = -39\,\text{m}\), \(v = \dfrac{(-39) \times 1}{-39 - 1} = \dfrac{39}{40}\,\text{m}\)

Since the jogger moves at a constant speed of \(5\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), after \(1\,\text{s}\) the position of the image \(v\) (for \(u = -39 + 5 = -34\)) is \((34/35)\,\text{m}\).

The shift in the position of image in \(1\,\text{s}\) is
\(\dfrac{39}{40} - \dfrac{34}{35} = \dfrac{1365 - 1360}{1400} = \dfrac{5}{1400} = \dfrac{1}{280}\,\text{m}\)

Therefore, the average speed of the image when the jogger is between \(39\,\text{m}\) and \(34\,\text{m}\) from the mirror, is \((1/280)\,\text{m s}^{-1}\)

Similarly, it can be seen that for \(u = -29\,\text{m}\), \(-19\,\text{m}\) and \(-9\,\text{m}\), the speed with which the image appears to move is
\(\dfrac{1}{150}\,\text{m s}^{-1},\ \dfrac{1}{60}\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) and \(\dfrac{1}{10}\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), respectively.

Although the jogger has been moving with a constant speed, the speed of his/her image appears to increase substantially as he/she moves closer to the mirror. This phenomenon can be noticed by any person sitting in a stationary car or a bus. In case of moving vehicles, a similar phenomenon could be observed if the vehicle in the rear is moving closer with a constant speed.

subtopic: Refraction at Spherical Surfaces and by Lenses
stem: Light from a point source in air falls on a spherical glass surface (\(n = 1.5\) and radius of curvature \(= 20\,\text{cm}\)). The distance of the light source from the glass surface is \(100\,\text{cm}\). At what position the image is formed?
solution:
We use the relation given by Eq. (9.16). Here
\(u = -100\,\text{cm}\), \(v = ?\), \(R = +20\,\text{cm}\), \(n_1 = 1\), and \(n_2 = 1.5\).

We then have
\(\dfrac{1.5}{v} + \dfrac{1}{100} = \dfrac{0.5}{20}\)

or \(v = +100\,\text{cm}\)

The image is formed at a distance of \(100\,\text{cm}\) from the glass surface, in the direction of incident light.

subtopic: Refraction at Spherical Surfaces and by Lenses
stem: A magician during a show makes a glass lens with \(n = 1.47\) disappear in a trough of liquid. What is the refractive index of the liquid? Could the liquid be water?
solution: The refractive index of the liquid must be equal to \(1.47\) in order to make the lens disappear. This means \(n_1 = n_2\). This gives \(1/f = 0\) or \(f \to \infty\). The lens in the liquid will act like a plane sheet of glass. No, the liquid is not water. It could be glycerine.

subtopic: Refraction at Spherical Surfaces and by Lenses
stem: (i) If \(f = 0.5\,\text{m}\) for a glass lens, what is the power of the lens? (ii) The radii of curvature of the faces of a double convex lens are \(10\,\text{cm}\) and \(15\,\text{cm}\). Its focal length is \(12\,\text{cm}\). What is the refractive index of glass? (iii) A convex lens has \(20\,\text{cm}\) focal length in air. What is focal length in water? (Refractive index of air-water \(= 1.33\), refractive index for air-glass \(= 1.5\).)
solution:
(i) Power \(= +2\) dioptre.

(ii) Here, we have \(f = +12\,\text{cm}\), \(R_1 = +10\,\text{cm}\), \(R_2 = -15\,\text{cm}\). Refractive index of air is taken as unity. We use the lens formula of Eq. (9.22). The sign convention has to be applied for \(f\), \(R_1\) and \(R_2\).

Substituting the values, we have
\(\dfrac{1}{12} = (n - 1)\left(\dfrac{1}{10} - \dfrac{1}{-15}\right)\)

This gives \(n = 1.5\).

(iii) For a glass lens in air, \(n_2 = 1.5\), \(n_1 = 1\), \(f = +20\,\text{cm}\). Hence, the lens formula gives
\(\dfrac{1}{20} = 0.5\left[\dfrac{1}{R_1} - \dfrac{1}{R_2}\right]\)

For the same glass lens in water, \(n_2 = 1.5\), \(n_1 = 1.33\). Therefore,
\(\dfrac{1.33}{f} = (1.5 - 1.33)\left[\dfrac{1}{R_1} - \dfrac{1}{R_2}\right]\)

Combining these two equations, we find \(f = +78.2\,\text{cm}\).

subtopic: Refraction at Spherical Surfaces and by Lenses
stem: Find the position of the image formed by the lens combination given in the Fig. 9.20. [Fig. 9.20 shows an object O on the principal axis, \(30\,\text{cm}\) to the left of the first of three thin lenses of focal lengths \(f = +10\,\text{cm}\), \(-10\,\text{cm}\) and \(+30\,\text{cm}\); the first and second lenses are \(5\,\text{cm}\) apart and the second and third are \(10\,\text{cm}\) apart.]
solution:
Image formed by the first lens
\(\dfrac{1}{v_1} - \dfrac{1}{u_1} = \dfrac{1}{f_1}\)

\(\dfrac{1}{v_1} - \dfrac{1}{-30} = \dfrac{1}{10}\)

or \(v_1 = 15\,\text{cm}\)

The image formed by the first lens serves as the object for the second. This is at a distance of \((15 - 5)\,\text{cm} = 10\,\text{cm}\) to the right of the second lens. Though the image is real, it serves as a virtual object for the second lens, which means that the rays appear to come from it for the second lens.

\(\dfrac{1}{v_2} - \dfrac{1}{10} = \dfrac{1}{-10}\)

or \(v_2 = \infty\)

The virtual image is formed at an infinite distance to the left of the second lens. This acts as an object for the third lens.

\(\dfrac{1}{v_3} - \dfrac{1}{u_3} = \dfrac{1}{f_3}\)

or \(\dfrac{1}{v_3} = \dfrac{1}{\infty} + \dfrac{1}{30}\)

or \(v_3 = 30\,\text{cm}\)

The final image is formed \(30\,\text{cm}\) to the right of the third lens.
_note: The printed stem is only 'Find the position of the image formed by the lens combination given in the Fig. 9.20.' — every datum (the three focal lengths, the 30 cm object distance and the 5 cm / 10 cm separations) is printed INSIDE Fig. 9.20 and nowhere in the sentence. The figure's data is therefore appended to the stem in square brackets so the row is answerable on its own; no _figure crop is requested because the book's printed solution is transcribed in full here.

stem: A small candle, \(2.5\,\text{cm}\) in size is placed at \(27\,\text{cm}\) in front of a concave mirror of radius of curvature \(36\,\text{cm}\). At what distance from the mirror should a screen be placed in order to obtain a sharp image? Describe the nature and size of the image. If the candle is moved closer to the mirror, how would the screen have to be moved?

A \(4.5\,\text{cm}\) needle is placed \(12\,\text{cm}\) away from a convex mirror of focal length \(15\,\text{cm}\). Give the location of the image and the magnification. Describe what happens as the needle is moved farther from the mirror.

A tank is filled with water to a height of \(12.5\,\text{cm}\). The apparent depth of a needle lying at the bottom of the tank is measured by a microscope to be \(9.4\,\text{cm}\). What is the refractive index of water? Predict the angle of refraction in glass when the angle of incidence in water is \(45^\circ\) with the normal to a water-glass interface [Fig. 9.27(c)].

A small bulb is placed at the bottom of a tank containing water to a depth of \(80\,\text{cm}\). What is the area of the surface of water through which light from the bulb can emerge out? Refractive index of water is \(1.33\). (Consider the bulb to be a point source.)

A prism is made of glass of unknown refractive index. A parallel beam of light is incident on a face of the prism. The angle of minimum deviation is measured to be \(40^\circ\). What is the refractive index of the material of the prism? The refracting angle of the prism is \(60^\circ\). If the prism is placed in water (refractive index \(1.33\)), predict the new angle of minimum deviation of a parallel beam of light.
